name: Germany
summary: Children, the spouse and, if there are no children, the parents have a money claim of half their intestate share that a will cannot remove. A foreign national resident can choose their national law under the EU Succession Regulation. Germany has no trust law, but a Stiftung (including a family foundation) can be set up.
reserved_share: Pflichtteil: descendants, spouse or registered partner, and parents (only if there are no descendants) get a money claim of half their statutory share (BGB art. 2303). Lifetime gifts within 10 years are added back, decreasing yearly (BGB art. 2325).
foreign_law_note: Reg. 650/2012 art. 22 allows a choice of nationality law, which removes the German Pflichtteil; the public-policy exception (art. 35) is rarely used against it.
trust_note: Germany has no domestic trust law and is not party to the Hague Trusts Convention. The HCCH status table lists no signature or ratification for this state; the Convention is not in force here. Foreign trusts are treated for inheritance tax like a transfer to a foundation, which usually means tax class III (Inheritance Tax Act, ErbStG). Foundations are governed by BGB art. 80-88a, reformed on 1 July 2023; a Familienstiftung is allowed, and the ErbStG charges a substitute inheritance tax on it every 30 years (art. 1 para. 1 no. 4).
open_questions: Exact ErbStG sub-paragraphs for foreign trusts were not looked up.
